title: The Unsaid Radiators
premise: Noor Winterbourne, once a piano prodigy who vanished from the conservatory at nineteen, returns a decade later not as a student but as its night janitor, cataloguing in a private notebook all the sentences she never said — to her estranged mentor, to her sister, to herself. When the house where she grew up goes to public auction, she discovers her mentor is the buyer and that the deed hinges on an untranslated letter her mother left behind, written in a language only Noor can read. Translating it truthfully will expose the betrayal that ended her career; translating it falsely will save the man who destroyed her but cost her sister everything. In the end Noor reads the letter aloud at the auction, unedited, choosing truth over loyalty — and walks out owning nothing but the unsaid, finally said.
about_author: R. M. Winterbourne is the pen name of a former conservatory custodian who spent eleven years sweeping concert halls before publishing a first story collection praised for its 'silences you can hear.' The Unsaid Radiators is their debut novel, written largely on breaks between shifts.

chapters.title: Inventory of Small Silences
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. We meet her mopping the conservatory floor at night, past the practice rooms where students play pieces she once played better. She begins entry #1 of her notebook of unsaid things. Emotional beat: quiet resignation masking grief, establishing the ritual that structures her life.

chapters.title: The Auction Notice
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. A flyer pinned to the community board announces the sale of her childhood home. Her hands shake; a student notices and asks if she used to play. Emotional beat: the past breaking through the present like water through plaster, and the first crack in her careful anonymity.

chapters.title: What My Sister Kept
chapters.summary: Sister Amal's POV. Amal has been paying taxes on the empty house for years, believing Noor abandoned the family after the scandal. She confronts Noor outside the conservatory. Emotional beat: resentment braided with longing; we learn the sisters' silence has two authors.

chapters.title: The Buyer
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. At the pre-auction viewing, Noor finds Master Elias Voss, her old mentor, inspecting the house — he intends to buy it, and he recognizes her instantly. He asks, gently, for a favor. Emotional beat: dread and the dangerous warmth of being seen by someone who once mattered.

chapters.title: The Letter in the Piano Bench
chapters.summary: Amal's POV. Clearing the house, Amal finds their mother's letter hidden in the piano bench, written in Farsi shorthand only Noor was taught. Voss claims the right to read it first. Emotional beat: the object of the whole story surfaces, and every character's stake sharpens.

chapters.title: Entry Forty-Seven
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Flashback chapter: the night at nineteen when Voss took credit for her composition and let her be expelled for 'plagiarism' rather than admit his own theft. She wrote the truth then and never sent it. Emotional beat: the wound reopened; the reader now knows exactly what the translation could destroy.

chapters.title: Terms of Silence
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. Dying, Voss offers Noor the house free and clear if she translates the letter as 'a farewell blessing' — which it partly is. He frames it as mercy, maybe believes it. Emotional beat: seductive moral fog; loyalty and self-preservation whispering in one voice.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Alone in the empty house overnight, Noor works through the letter line by line until she reaches the sentence: her mother knew what Voss did, and forgave him — but asked Noor to say so aloud, because forgiveness withheld in silence rots both people. Emotional beat: stillness before the storm; the choice crystallizes.

chapters.title: Auction Day
chapters.summary: Noor's POV (with Amal present). Bidding opens; Voss watches from the back. Instead of bidding, Noor stands and reads the entire letter aloud, including the sentence about Voss, in front of the room. The auction collapses into uproar; Voss neither denies nor flees. Emotional beat: climax — exposure, relief, terror, and the strange lightness of a finished sentence.

chapters.title: Everything Said
chapters.summary: Amal's POV closing with Noor's final notebook entry. The sisters sit in the sold house one last time; Amal plays the upright piano left behind, badly, and Noor corrects her fingering — the first teaching either has offered in years. Entry #1 is crossed out. Emotional beat: resolution without repair — justice done, relationships beginning again from honesty instead of silence.
